output.myth: Ennu the Kite-Wright made a gull once, of sailcloth and goose-bone, and gave it to a girl on the windward cliff who had asked the wind a question and got no answer. The gull flew well. It went up past the goats and past the nesting ledges until it hung over the sea. Then Tavo came along the cliff laughing, as he does, and took one wing in his teeth and tore it. The gull hung there with one wing, wobbling. Aun saw it from the Lamp Road and wanted to know how far it would go, so he cut the string with his knife. That is why the kite lies up in the north, its head toward Hesk, its tail still trailing down toward the islands like a rope nobody pulled. The girl still looks up when the wind goes round to the north. Hesk keeps count of the string she lost, and says nothing.
output.verse:
Ennu's gull of cloth
Tavo tore one wing; string held
Hesk still winds the thread
